title: Lagrange's Theorem OQ-01: The Sylow Theorems as Partial Converse
description: Formal proof of all three Sylow theorems (existence, conjugacy, counting) as a partial converse to Lagrange's theorem, plus Cauchy's theorem, all from Mathlib.

meta.author: Lean Genius
originalContributions: Unified formal presentation of all three Sylow theorems connecting to Lagrange's theorem context
Explicit statement that n_p ≡ 1 mod p using Sylow.card_sylow_modEq_one
Partial converse to Lagrange: p^k | |G| implies subgroup of order p^k via Sylow.exists_subgroup_card_pow_prime
Cauchy's theorem as corollary of Sylow existence

overview.historicalContext: Joseph-Louis Lagrange first observed in his 1771 work on algebraic equations that the number of distinct values a rational function takes under permutations of its variables divides $n!$—the seeds of the theorem bearing his name. The result was fully articulated in the language of abstract groups by Arthur Cayley and others in the 19th century. Peter Ludwig Mejdell Sylow (1832–1918), a Norwegian mathematician, proved his foundational theorems in the landmark 1872 paper 'Théorèmes sur les groupes de substitutions' (Mathematische Annalen), working in the era when groups were primarily thought of as permutation groups on finite sets. The modern abstract formulation came through the work of Georg Frobenius, William Burnside (whose 1897 'Theory of Groups of Finite Order' systematized the theory), and Helmut Wielandt, who gave an elegant elementary proof via a counting argument on $p$-element subsets in 1959. Sylow Theorem I (existence) generalizes Augustin-Louis Cauchy's 1845 result—that $p \mid |G|$ implies an element of order $p$—from primes to prime powers. The three Sylow theorems together form the cornerstone of finite group classification: they reduce the question of whether certain subgroups exist (Lagrange's converse problem) to the prime-power case, and their counting and conjugacy constraints can force groups of specific orders to be cyclic or otherwise tightly structured.
overview.problemStatement: Formally state and prove all three Sylow theorems: (I) existence of Sylow $p$-subgroups ($p^k \mid |G|$ implies a subgroup of order $p^k$), (II) all Sylow $p$-subgroups are conjugate, (III) the count $n_p$ satisfies $n_p \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$ and $n_p \mid [G:P]$. Also prove the partial converse to Lagrange ($p^k \mid |G|$ implies a subgroup of order $p^k$) and Cauchy's theorem ($p \mid |G|$ implies an element of order $p$).
overview.proofStrategy: All results are extracted from Mathlib's group theory library (`Mathlib.GroupTheory.Sylow`). Sylow existence uses `Sylow.nonempty`; the Sylow order formula uses `Sylow.card_eq_multiplicity`; conjugacy uses `Sylow.conj_eq` with an explicit `aesop`-assisted computation of the conjugation map; counting uses `Sylow.card_sylow_dvd_index` and `Sylow.card_sylow_modEq_one`. The partial converse uses `Sylow.exists_subgroup_card_pow_prime`. Cauchy's theorem uses `exists_prime_orderOf_dvd_card`. The file's role is to assemble these Mathlib building blocks into a single coherent narrative around the Lagrange converse question.
keyInsights: $A_4$ (order 12) has no subgroup of order 6, showing the converse to Lagrange fails for composite divisors—this is why the Sylow theorems restrict to prime power divisors.
Sylow $p$-subgroups are *maximal* $p$-subgroups: their order is $p^{v_p(|G|)}$ where $v_p$ is the $p$-adic valuation, i.e., the full $p$-power part of the group order.

Conjugacy of Sylow subgroups (Theorem II) implies uniqueness when $n_p = 1$, in which case the unique Sylow $p$-subgroup is *normal* in $G$. This normality criterion is the key tool for proving groups of order $pq$ (with $p \nmid q-1$) are cyclic.

Cauchy's theorem ($p \mid |G|$ implies an element of order $p$) is a corollary of Sylow existence—the Sylow $p$-subgroup has order $p^k \geq p$, and its non-identity elements have order dividing $p^k$.

The counting constraint $n_p \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$ from Theorem III comes from analyzing the action of a Sylow $p$-subgroup $P$ on the set of all Sylow $p$-subgroups by conjugation: the fixed points under this action are exactly the conjugates of $P$ by itself, and the orbit-stabilizer theorem gives $n_p \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$.
prerequisites: p-adic valuation and prime factorization of group orders

sections.title: Sylow Theorems as Partial Converse to Lagrange
sections.summary: States the research question: Lagrange's theorem says |H| | |G|, but the converse fails (A₄ has no order-6 subgroup). The Sylow theorems provide the sharpest partial converse: for every prime power divisor p^k of |G|, a subgroup of order p^k exists.

sections.title: Imports and Namespace Setup
sections.summary: Imports all of Mathlib (for access to Sylow theory) and opens the Subgroup and Fintype namespaces. Declares G as an abstract finite group via type class constraints.

sections.title: Part I: Lagrange's Theorem
sections.summary: Three Lagrange-related theorems: card H | card G (Lagrange); the index formula card G = card H * H.index; and order_dvd_card (every element order divides |G|). All one-line proofs delegating to Mathlib.

sections.title: Part II: Sylow Existence (First Sylow Theorem)
sections.summary: Three theorems: sylow_exists (Sylow p-subgroups exist for every prime p); sylow_card_eq (the Sylow p-subgroup order is p^{v_p(|G|)}); sylow_order_dvd (the Sylow subgroup order divides |G|, as a special case of Lagrange).

sections.title: Part III: Sylow Conjugacy (Second Sylow Theorem)
sections.summary: sylow_conjugate: for any two Sylow p-subgroups P, Q, there exists g ∈ G such that Q = gPg⁻¹. Proved using Sylow.conj_eq and a brief aesop-assisted rewrite to match the Subgroup.map formulation.

sections.title: Part IV: Sylow Counting (Third Sylow Theorem)
sections.summary: Two counting theorems: sylow_count_dvd_index (n_p divides the index [G:P]); sylow_count_mod_p (n_p ≡ 1 mod p). The latter uses Sylow.card_sylow_modEq_one and .out to extract the Nat.ModEq equivalence.

sections.title: Part V: Partial Converse to Lagrange and Cauchy's Theorem
sections.summary: partial_converse_lagrange: for any prime power p^k dividing |G|, there is a subgroup of order p^k (via Sylow.exists_subgroup_card_pow_prime). cauchy_theorem: p | |G| implies an element of order p (via exists_prime_orderOf_dvd_card).

conclusion.summary: A 141-line Lean 4 file proving 11 theorems with 0 sorries and 0 axioms, all sourced from Mathlib, covering Lagrange's theorem, all three Sylow theorems, and Cauchy's theorem within the namespace LagrangeOQ01.
conclusion.implications: The Sylow theorems are among the most powerful tools in finite group theory. Together with Lagrange's theorem, they form the backbone of the order-based analysis of finite groups: Lagrange constrains subgroup orders to divisors of $|G|$, while Sylow guarantees subgroups for all prime-power divisors and constrains their count. These results underpin the classification of groups of small order — for example, every group of order $pq$ with $p < q$ primes and $p \nmid q-1$ is cyclic, derived from Sylow counting and normality. The result also connects to deep structure theorems: the Schur-Zassenhaus theorem, Hall's theorem for solvable groups (generalizing Sylow from prime powers to Hall numbers), and ultimately the classification of finite simple groups.
openQuestions: Formalize the application: classify groups of order $pq$ (p < q primes) using Sylow theory — show such groups are cyclic when $p \nmid q-1$.
Prove that $A_4$ has no subgroup of order 6 in Lean 4 (the canonical counterexample to the converse of Lagrange).
Formalize Hall's theorem: for solvable groups, a Hall $\pi$-subgroup exists for every set $\pi$ of primes — the full generalization of the Sylow existence theorem.
